brief.head: Bad bankers
brief.text: Finance means pro­cess­ing in­for­ma­tion, fore­cast­ing and tak­ing risks, Ajay Shah said, and bu­reau­crats have no in­cen­tive to do it. State med­dling in fi­nance is “a dis­mal mess”. {109-C07}

brief.head: The 99 per cent
brief.text: Lant Pritchett found that human wel­fare[[x5]][[x4]] in­di­ca­tors cor­re­late around 99 per cent with per capita GDP, Amit Varma said. Redistribution and wel­farism are left the re­main­ing one per cent. {109-R08}

brief.head: Training the gut
brief.text: Woken at 3 a.m., Ajay Shah said, his mind runs on the price sys­tem and gen­eral equi­lib­rium. Intuitions can be re­trained, Amit Varma said, by “light bulb mo­ments”. {109-C03}

brief.head: Credit means debt
brief.text: Restate a claim from the other side, Amit Varma said, quot­ing Henry Hazlitt: more credit means more debt, sub­si­dies mean higher taxes, more ex­ports ul­ti­mately mean more im­ports. {109-C16}

brief.head: Mind the individual
brief.text: Think of real peo­ple, not ab­strac­tions such as the na­tion, Amit Varma said: Hazlitt traced many fal­la­cies to for­get­ting “the in­di­vid­u­als who make it up and give it mean­ing”. {109-C17}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah read Henry Hazlitt’s classic
lead.head: A 1946 lesson, still unlearnt

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 109

body: Henry Hazlitt pub­lished *Economics in One Lesson* in 1946. In later edi­tions, Amit Varma said, he added chap­ters but did not change a word of the orig­i­nal text, be­cause its prin­ci­ples still held.
It was the first of a planned se­ries in which the hosts take apart one book at a time, and Varma said its fal­la­cies are still being com­mit­ted today.
He read out Hazlitt’s own di­ag­no­sis from 1946: “This book is an anal­y­sis of eco­nomic fal­la­cies that are at last so preva­lent that they have be­come al­most a new or­tho­doxy.”
They sur­vive, Varma said, be­cause economics’ deep­est truths are coun­ter­in­tu­itive. Intuition says the world is zero-sum and must be run from the top down.
## The art of eco­nom­ics

The les­son of the title fits in two sen­tences, which Varma read aloud: “The art of eco­nom­ics con­sists in look­ing not merely at the im­me­di­ate but at the longer ef­fects of any act or pol­icy. It con­sists in trac­ing the con­se­quences of that pol­icy not merely for one group, but for all groups.” {109-C01}
Hazlitt took the method from the es­say­ist Frédéric Bastiat, whose para­ble of the bro­ken win­dow is a les­son in what goes un­seen.

A boy breaks a shop win­dow, and a by­stander calls it good for the econ­omy, be­cause the glazier gets paid. Unseen is what the shop­keeper would have spent the money on in­stead: a suit, and through it the tai­lor.
That, Varma said, is op­por­tu­nity cost. The same logic dis­poses of the claim that war is good for the econ­omy.
## The un­seen bill
The rest of the book ap­plies the les­son chap­ter by chap­ter. Public works mean taxes: for every pub­lic job a bridge cre­ates, a pri­vate job is de­stroyed some­where else.

Taxes dis­cour­age pro­duc­tion, and Varma trans­lated them into time: “If you are taxed one third of your in­come, that means that for four months of the year you are work­ing for the gov­ern­ment of India, you’re not work­ing for your­self.” {109-C06}

The fear that ma­chines de­stroy jobs has re­curred from the Luddites to today’s wor­ries about AI. Varma had no pa­tience for it: “There’s never been an ex­cep­tion, and there is no rea­son to be­lieve there will be an ex­cep­tion this time.” {109-C08}
Ajay Shah added that a so­ci­ety can only con­sume what it pro­duces, and that new tech­nol­ogy spreads slowly, leav­ing time to ad­just.
## Rent and com­pas­sion
The hosts saved their long­est ar­gu­ment for rent con­trol, a chap­ter Hazlitt added in 1961.
Price con­trols al­ways cause scarcity, Varma said. Marine Drive in Bombay has sprawl­ing flats let for a few hun­dred ru­pees a month, in di­lap­i­dated build­ings no­body main­tains. {109-C13}

The sub­ject is back in the news. Zohran Mamdani, who won New York’s Democratic may­oral pri­mary, wants rent con­trol. Varma found him charm­ing and his eco­nomic poli­cies “a throw­back to the worst ex­cesses of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury”.
Such schemes let peo­ple project virtue, Varma ar­gued. True com­pas­sion asks whether a pol­icy helps the peo­ple it means to help, and these, he said, hurt the poor.

Varma’s guid­ing frame­work, he said, Adam Smith had stated long be­fore him: what is pru­dence in a fam­ily can scarcely be folly in a king­dom. “All de­cent peo­ple, in our per­sonal deal­ings, we are lib­er­tar­ian,” Varma said. The task is to carry those val­ues over to the state. {109-C20}

second.label: Depression economics
second.head: Autobahns to recovery
second.deck: Ajay Shah finds one exception to Henry Hazlitt’s case against make-work spending

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Great Depression exception

body: Ajay Shah broadly agrees with Henry Hazlitt that make-work spend­ing is a mis­take. He made one ex­cep­tion: the Great Depression.

Mistakes in mon­e­tary pol­icy had col­lapsed the money sup­ply, and a quar­ter of all banks went bust. Firms that lost their bank could not eas­ily start again with an­other. Adolf Hitler then bor­rowed to rearm and build au­to­bahns, and the jobs and re-spending pulled Germany out of the slump, Shah said. {109-S03}

Amit Varma replied that Hazlitt’s tar­get was gov­ern­ments that build what is not needed “under the guise of pro­duc­ing em­ploy­ment”. {#guise} On the Depression, he pointed to con­trary ac­counts by Amity Shlaes and Thomas Sowell[[x2]][[x1]].

quote.text: He ac­tu­ally wanted the arms, he ac­tu­ally wanted the au­to­bahns.

third.head: Painting by numbers

pic.caption: Amit Varma (right) on the painting made in Excel, with Ajay Shah

body: Amit Varma had a quiz for Ajay Shah. He showed him a paint­ing by the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi and asked what medium it was made in. Shah had no idea. {109-S07}
“He made it using a tech­nol­ogy you re­ferred to five min­utes ago,” Varma said. “He made it using Microsoft Excel.”

Shah had just been ar­gu­ing that new tech­nolo­gies spread slowly. Spreadsheets ex­isted by the mid-1970s, he said, yet large parts of Indian busi­ness still lack even basic spread­sheet skills. {#spreadsheets}

Varma had in­tro­duced the quiz with Arthur C. Clarke’s line[[x3]] that any suf­fi­ciently ad­vanced tech­nol­ogy is in­dis­tin­guish­able from magic. The word de­feated him. It came out as “in­ter­na­tion­al­iza­tion from magic”. {109-J11} A spread­sheet, it turned out, could also be a paint­brush.

box.title: The book on the table
box.text: Lant Pritchett told Amit Varma this was the book that turned him onto eco­nom­ics. Henry Hazlitt, “a great es­say­ist and thinker”[[x6]], pub­lished it in 1946 and, through two later edi­tions, never changed a word of the orig­i­nal chap­ters. {109-R01}

sections.label: The book
sections.head: Lights you can’t switch off
sections.caption: why the book still matters
body: Every five episodes or so, Amit Varma an­nounced, the hosts will pick one book that shaped them and break it down. He began with Henry Hazlitt’s *Economics in One Lesson*. {#everyfive}

The book came out in 1946 and was an im­me­di­ate best­seller. Hazlitt added a chap­ter on rent con­trol in 1961, ex­panded it in 1978 and added a clos­ing chap­ter, but left the rest un­touched. Fundamental prin­ci­ples, Varma said, need lit­tle up­dat­ing, as in physics.

Such books are needed be­cause economics’ deep­est truths, such as spon­ta­neous order and pos­i­tive-sum ex­change, run against in­tu­ition. Intuition tells us the world is zero-sum and must be con­trolled from the top down. Varma no­ticed Ajay Shah smil­ing: “Because you are the man on the top con­trol­ling.” {109-J04}
## Seeing order ev­ery­where

Intuitions can be re­trained, Varma ar­gued, through light bulb mo­ments that can­not be un­done. {109-C03} His came from Friedrich Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, on how prices work.
Matt Ridley’s *The Evolution of Everything*[[x7]] showed him spon­ta­neous order run­ning through nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage and prices. “It is so mirac­u­lous,” he said. {109-R11}

~ The hosts, Varma said, try to throw light bulbs at the screen. Shah promptly imag­ined the mer­chan­dise: a can­non be­side the TV, fir­ing de­funct tung­sten bulbs at the viewer on Varma’s cue. {109-J05}

quote.text: You flick a switch and the light comes on. And you can never unsee what you have just seen.

sections.label: The parable
sections.head: The suit nobody saw
sections.caption: the broken window
body: Henry Hazlitt’s les­son sets two econ­o­mists side by side. “The bad econ­o­mist sees only what im­me­di­ately strikes the eye. The good econ­o­mist also looks be­yond,” Amit Varma read. {109-C01}

Hazlitt also mocked an un­named econ­o­mist who said that in the long run we are all dead. Ajay Shah guessed at once: “I love John Maynard Keynes dearly and one of his crimes was that he was wise, witty, and won­der­ful.” {109-J03}
## A win­dow and a war

Hazlitt drew on Frédéric Bastiat’s para­ble[[x9]][[x8]]. A boy breaks a shop win­dow, and a by­stander, in Varma’s telling “no doubt a wise Bengali econ­o­mist”, hails the glazier’s wind­fall as a stim­u­lus. {109-J06} Varma, a Bengali him­self, later said he does not like Bengali econ­o­mists ei­ther.

The un­seen half is the suit the shop­keeper would have bought, and the tai­lor who would have spent the money in turn. {109-C02} That is op­por­tu­nity cost, and the same logic sinks the claim that war, or re­build­ing ru­ined cities, is good for the econ­omy.
~ For Shah, the big­gest ex­am­ple is growth against re­dis­tri­bu­tion. Redistribution, he said, pits peo­ple against peo­ple: “This is a game of class war­fare.” {109-C04}

quote.text: What is not seen is what the shop­keeper would have done with the twenty ru­pees had he kept it with him­self.

sections.label: The taxman
sections.head: Where bridges can be built
sections.caption: bridges, taxes and time
body: Nothing the gov­ern­ment does is free, Amit Varma said: it is paid for in taxes, and so through co­er­cion[[x10]]. Henry Hazlitt’s chap­ter on pub­lic works shows the trade. “For every pub­lic job cre­ated by the bridge project, a pri­vate job has been de­stroyed some­where else.” {109-C05}
Once jobs be­come the goal, Hazlitt wrote, gov­ern­ments stop ask­ing where bridges must be built and ask where they can be built. Varma sees the same make-work logic in India’s NREGS.
## Months for the state

Taxes also dis­cour­age pro­duc­tion. Varma urged lis­ten­ers to count their taxes in months of work. {109-C06} Everyone pays, he said: the beg­gar at the traf­fic sig­nal buy­ing salt, the do­mes­tic help buy­ing soap. Inflation is a tax on the poor.
Under Indira Gandhi, he re­called, the peak per­sonal in­come tax rate[[x11]] was 95 or 97 per cent, an in­cen­tive to leave the coun­try or to hoard black money. {#peakrate}

~ Varma called India’s space pro­gramme a waste of money. Ajay Shah, tongue in cheek, called it real progress that India paid a for­eign com­pany to launch an Indian as­tro­naut: cheaper, with the same pro­pa­ganda value. Carried to its log­i­cal con­clu­sion, he said, “what you need is an AI video”. {109-J07}

art.caption: Amit Varma on bridges, taxes and time

sections.label: The machine
sections.head: Chicken in, cars out
sections.caption: machines, trade and jobs
body: Those who can­not re­mem­ber the past are con­demned to re­peat it, George Santayana wrote, and Amit Varma is tired of each new wave of techno­pho­bia, from the Luddites to today’s fears about AI. {109-J15}

Henry Hazlitt’s an­swer starts with Adam Smith’s pin-makers[[x12]]. A work­man with ma­chin­ery could make 4,800 pins a day where one with­out could scarcely make one, yet em­ploy­ment went up, not down. If sav­ing labour were bad, Hazlitt asked, why not carry freight on men’s backs?
## Magic at the port

Ajay Shah’s re­but­tal was that society’s ag­gre­gate con­sump­tion is its ag­gre­gate pro­duc­tion, so pro­duc­tiv­ity gains raise con­sump­tion per head. {109-C09} And adop­tion is slow. Driverless cars will re­place India’s driv­ers, he said, but over prob­a­bly 25 years. {#driverless}

Trade, he added, is a tech­nol­ogy too. Frozen chicken from Maharashtra’s poul­try farms leaves JNPT and comes back as elec­tric ve­hi­cles, a rival to Mahindra’s fac­tory at Igatpuri. {109-C10} To stop progress, you would have to shut down trade as well.
~ What turns change into con­flict is cul­ture, Shah ar­gued. Great so­ci­eties are “more Gandhiji and less Karl Marx”. {109-C11}

quote.text: So sit­ting at JNPT is a piece of magic that con­verts frozen chicken into elec­tric ve­hi­cles.

portraits.caption: Karl Marx
portraits.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain

sections.label: The landlord
sections.head: Rent frozen, capital dead
sections.caption: rent control and dead capital
body: Rent con­trol is back in the news.[[x13]] Zohran Mamdani, win­ner of New York’s Democratic may­oral pri­mary and son of Mira Nair, one of Amit Varma’s favourite film­mak­ers, wants it. Varma finds him charm­ing, con­demns the racist at­tacks on him and calls his poli­cies “a throw­back to the worst ex­cesses of the twen­ti­eth cen­tury”. {109-J20}

The seen ef­fect is that ten­ants are spared ris­ing rents. The un­seen ef­fects, Varma said, are that land­lords stop main­tain­ing build­ings, de­vel­op­ers stop build­ing, and ten­ants stop economis­ing on space. {109-C13}
## Dead cap­i­tal

Varma bor­rowed a con­cept from Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*: with­out title, land that peo­ple ef­fec­tively own can­not be bor­rowed against, so it is dead cap­i­tal. {109-R26} Rent con­trol, he ar­gued, turns liv­ing prop­erty into dead cap­i­tal: “It is equal to theft.”

Opponents of such schemes, Varma said, are made to sound evil. A tweet by Daniel Hannan re­minded him of a left­ist friend who once told him: “Amit, I didn’t re­alise you cared so much. I thought you’re lib­er­tar­ian, you don’t give a shit about peo­ple.” {109-S06}
~ Ajay Shah of­fered Mamdani the old line about com­mu­nism, the heart and the brain: “So give him a break.” Varma’s reply: “Thirty-four is old enough.” {109-J12}

quote.text: You have taken an apart­ment or a build­ing or a build­ing block or a neigh­bor­hood and you made it dead cap­i­tal.

portraits.caption: Hernando de Soto
portraits.credit: Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Five lenses for any policy
sections.caption: the Hazlitt toolkit
body: Amit Varma drew three broad lessons from the book. Look at longer ef­fects and at all groups. Think of in­di­vid­u­als, not ab­strac­tions such as the na­tion. {109-C17} And re­state every claim from the other side.

Then came a tool­kit: op­por­tu­nity cost, gen­eral wel­fare over in­ter­est groups, in­cen­tives and dis­tor­tions, the price sys­tem, and cap­i­tal for­ma­tion. The price sys­tem, Varma said, should be treated as sa­cred. {109-C19}
## Who pays, who gains

From his friend Suyash Rai, Varma took a warn­ing about cost-benefit sums. The cost falls on one group now, the ben­e­fit on an­other, often imag­ined and in the fu­ture. Demonetisation, he said, had no ben­e­fits at all. {109-C18}

His most im­por­tant frame­work, Varma said, was one Adam Smith had stated long be­fore him: what is pru­dence in a fam­ily can scarcely be folly in a king­dom. Friends at a restau­rant do not force each other to eat or to pay, he said, yet co­er­cion seems fine one level up, at the state. {109-C20}

~ Ajay Shah urged lis­ten­ers to read the book it­self: Varma telling its story, he said, was “one hun­dredth of read­ing the book”. {#hundredth} Asked about young Ajays run­ning around the world, Shah said they would soon get over the delu­sion “that there is any­thing here which is some­how spe­cial”. “Oh my god, such mod­esty,” said Varma.

quote.text: Prices are how we get in­for­ma­tion about what oth­ers can do for us and what we could pos­si­bly do for them.

And there­fore the truly com­pas­sion­ate peo­ple are those who think of the out­comes and they ask the ques­tion that are you ac­tu­ally help­ing the peo­ple you’re try­ing to help or are you hurt­ing them?

p3.title: Tales of the unseen
p3.deck: A bureaucrat, a father, a satellite and a forest, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a bureaucrat, a pun and a twist
stories.head: The industry that saved itself
body: Some years ago, Amit Varma got talk­ing to a se­nior bu­reau­crat in a West Bengal min­istry. At the time, the man was look­ing after the jute in­dus­try.
Varma asked him what the think­ing was. The jute in­dus­try was not doing well. It was an in­dige­nous in­dus­try, “our thing”, and the gov­ern­ment had to keep it alive.
The bureaucrat’s tech­no­cratic mind, as Varma put it, was full of sub­si­dies, price con­trols and grants of land.

“And I was like, Why? Why does the gov­ern­ment have a role to play in it?” Varma re­called. {109-S04} Let sup­ply and de­mand de­cide, he ar­gued. Whatever is done for jute comes at the cost of some­thing else, and no­body sees the jobs and wel­fare lost there.
Midway through the retelling, Varma slipped in a Hindi pun on jute and jhoot, a lie, and re­fused to ex­plain it. Ajay Shah got it “forty-five mil­lisec­onds later”, by his own count. {109-J09}

This is what Henry Hazlitt called sav­ing the X in­dus­try[[x14]]. Varma said such think­ing has faded in the West but per­sists in India. Shah added that China runs the same play­book, “just done 5x more ex­treme than India”. {#china}

Then Shah de­liv­ered the twist. Jute, he said, is now doing ex­tremely well, be­cause global tech­no­log­i­cal forces made the world want more of it, and that has noth­ing to do with the gov­ern­ment. {#jute}
~ Varma had not ex­pected that. It was, he said, “one more thing to be proud of”.
stories.why: Any favour to one in­dus­try is paid for by oth­ers, whose lost jobs go un­seen. {109-C12} The punch­line: jute thrived be­cause the wider world wanted it, not be­cause any­one saved it.
stories.postscript: The fix­a­tion got Varma’s goat, he said, adding: “I should be care­ful about what I say be­cause I don’t have a goat.”

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the jute bureaucrat

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on his father’s Bombay, before rent control
stories.head: A flat in fifteen minutes
body: Around 1976, when Ajay Shah was about ten, his fam­ily of six would sit at the din­ner table and talk for hours about the world. Bombay was in the throes of rent con­trol[[x15]], and rent­ing any­thing was es­sen­tially im­pos­si­ble.

One evening his fa­ther told them about ar­riv­ing in the city in 1942, the year Gandhiji launched the Quit India move­ment. “When I first came to Bombay, you could just walk around the street and within fif­teen min­utes you could rent a flat.” {109-S02}
The chil­dren were wide-eyed. To kids like them, Shah said, rent­ing a house eas­ily was an un­be­liev­able con­cept.

~ Rent con­trol had ended a free mar­ket. Nobody wanted to let out prop­erty, and by the 1970s the old ease had van­ished. Today, Shah said, mod­ern legal en­gi­neer­ing makes rent­ing far more fea­si­ble.
stories.why: Rent control’s deep­est dam­age is in­vis­i­ble to those born after it. A gen­er­a­tion can grow up think­ing a bro­ken hous­ing mar­ket is nor­mal, in a city where rent­ing was once easy. It has been a dis­as­ter, Amit Varma said, wher­ever it has been tried. {#disaster}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on his father’s Bombay

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Barun Mitra’s campaign for tribal land
stories.head: From Google Earth to pakka homes
body: About twenty years ago, Amit Varma said, the hosts’ friend Barun Mitra joined a move­ment[[x16]] in Gujarat to win prop­erty rights for trib­als. The chal­lenge was proof: how long they had lived there, and where the bound­aries lay.
The an­swer came from space. Using his­tor­i­cal Google Earth satel­lite im­agery, the cam­paign­ers showed how long the trib­als had been on the land, and the trib­als got their rights.

“And the first thing they did, when they got the rights, was made pakka hous­ing for them­selves. They built toi­lets for them­selves,” Varma said. {109-S05} In the past they had not, be­cause they could be pushed out at any time.
~ The story is told in *India Awakes*, a doc­u­men­tary pre­sented by Johan Norberg. {109-R30}
stories.why: Ownership changes in­cen­tives overnight. People do not in­vest in land they could lose, and once it is theirs, they build. It is the cure for what Hernando de Soto calls dead cap­i­tal. {109-R26}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Barun Mitra’s satellites

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s holiday, told at his own expense
stories.head: What goes up over Bir
body: Ajay Shah opened the episode in­sist­ing he had noth­ing as ex­cit­ing as Amit Varma’s se­cret project to re­port. Then he de­scribed a few days in Bir[[x17]].
There he spent time with the trail run­ner Sanat Sachdev, “just all round cool per­son”, who got him think­ing about run­ning in the moun­tains. He also took a two-hour tan­dem paraglid­ing ride.
At the high­est point the ride turned rocky. “The guy be­hind me, the pilot, gen­tly in­structed me on how to stick my head out and puke on the for­est below,” Shah said. {109-S01}
~ “Are you the first econ­o­mist to puke on a for­est?” Varma asked. {109-J02} Shah shrugged it off: any­body who does se­ri­ous paraglid­ing faces mo­tion sick­ness.

quote.text: If you puke on a for­est but no­body sees it, did you puke?

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the paragliding ride

quiz.q: In Bastiat’s parable, what might the shopkeeper have bought with the money spent on his window?
quiz.a: A suit, so the tai­lor, not the glazier, would have got the money.

quiz.q: Hazlitt mocked an economist who said “In the long run we are all dead”. Whom did Ajay Shah name?
quiz.a: John Maynard Keynes, whom Shah loves dearly, crimes and all.

quiz.q: Taxed a third of your income, how much of the year are you working for the government?
quiz.a: Four months of every year, which Amit Varma called part-time slav­ery.

quiz.q: Where does Ajay Shah locate the “piece of magic” that turns frozen chicken into electric vehicles?
quiz.a: At JNPT, the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust: trade, he says, is a tech­nol­ogy.

quiz.q: What medium did the artist Tatsuo Horiuchi use for the painting Amit Varma showed Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Microsoft Excel, the very spread­sheet tech­nol­ogy Shah had men­tioned five min­utes ear­lier.

quiz.q: What did Gujarat’s tribals build first after winning rights to their land with satellite evidence?
quiz.a: Pakka houses and toi­lets, which they never built while they could be evicted.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 109. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Henry Hazlitt (work-for-hire, CC BY 3.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Mahatma Gandhi (Elliott & Fry, public domain); Karl Marx (John Jabez Edwin Mayall, public domain); Hernando de Soto (Institute for Liberty and Democracy, CC BY-SA 3.0); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Thomas Sowell (Internet Archive Book Images, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: Basic Economics
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell’s book for learn­ing the basic con­cepts of eco­nom­ics in sim­ple lan­guage, one of Amit’s go-to an­swers when asked for a sin­gle fun­da­men­tal book; he says to read all of Sowell’s books.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Beware of These Five Fallacies! (Ep 45 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How in­stincts evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes mis­lead us in large, com­plex so­ci­eties: zero-sum think­ing, top-down think­ing, blind­ness to spon­ta­neous order and the pull of strong lead­ers.

shelf.title: Stay Away From Luxury Beliefs (Ep 46 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: On be­liefs im­ported from rich-world dis­course that make their hold­ers feel vir­tu­ous while hurt­ing the peo­ple they claim to help, such as the min­i­mum wage, or op­pos­ing sweat­shops that beat every other op­tion work­ers have.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Price System (Ep 66 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the price sys­tem should be treated as sa­cred: price con­trols al­most al­ways lead to short­ages, and free prices let a shock work it­self out through many small ad­just­ments rather than one big col­lapse.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Ep 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Economic growth is enough and only economic growth is enough
shelf.creator: Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: Pritchett’s paper, which Amit calls a mas­ter­piece of data and clear lan­guage, finds that human wel­fare in­di­ca­tors from health on­wards cor­re­late at around 99% with per capita GDP, leav­ing re­dis­tri­bu­tion and wel­farism a sliver of the story.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Ep 41 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley finds the same bot­tom-up process, with no plan­ner or de­signer, be­hind nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, prices, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything (Ep 96 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Matt Ridley, a com­pan­ion to his book, on how order emerges bot­tom-up with­out cen­tral de­sign, across bi­ol­ogy, cul­ture and mar­kets.

shelf.title: That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Ep 57 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Ep 25 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Ep 55 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles chal­lenge to India’s op­ti­mism about every new road and air­port: in­fra­struc­ture has di­min­ish­ing re­turns, and big re­cent gains brought no com­pa­ra­ble rise in FDI, man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports or jobs.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
shelf.creator: Amity Shlaes
shelf.why: A con­trary his­tory of the Great Depression that Amit has a lot of sym­pa­thy for: gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tions, not the stock-market crash, turned a down­turn into a de­pres­sion.

shelf.title: Rethinking Innovation Policy (Ep 59 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why re­search fund­ing in India is ‘a truly bad space’, and the al­ter­na­tive: an in­dus­try-neutral ap­proach that con­tracts R&D out through grants to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms rather than hav­ing bu­reau­crats pick sec­tors.

shelf.title: Who Lends to the Indian State?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah & co-authors
shelf.why: XKDR Forum’s paper, the first to mea­sure India’s fi­nan­cial re­pres­sion: 95% of the Indian state’s bor­row­ing is co­erced out of the fi­nan­cial sys­tem, which makes its debt look cheaper than it re­ally is.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (Ep 95 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: Is Globalization Doomed? (Ep 96 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The sec­ond part of the glob­al­i­sa­tion two-parter: how the open in­ter­na­tional order broke down, mainly be­cause China, and to a lesser ex­tent India, didn’t play by the rules, and why trade bar­ri­ers crip­ple man­u­fac­tur­ing.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: Prices, Fast and Slow
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s piece, which Amit calls won­der­ful, on what hap­pens when the state messes with prices.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price in the econ­omy and should be set by the mar­ket: rig­ging it to make ex­porters look com­pet­i­tive is a trans­fer from the poor, and man­ag­ing it in­vites cur­rency crises.

shelf.title: Episode 14 of The Seen and the Unseen: Rent Control
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: Alex Tabarrok’s short primer on the un­seen con­se­quences of rent con­trol, with the vivid case of rent-controlled New York look­ing like a bombed-out city.

shelf.title: The Mystery of Capital
shelf.creator: Hernando de Soto
shelf.why: De Soto’s idea of ‘dead capital’: with­out prop­erty rights, un­ti­tled slum homes and re­stricted land are worth some­thing but can’t be bor­rowed against or in­vested, so the poor can’t turn what they own into cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C. Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Daniel Hannan’s tweet on the left and compassion
shelf.creator: Daniel Hannan
shelf.why: It ar­gues that the left’s defin­ing trait is not com­pas­sion but the con­vic­tion that com­pas­sion is unique to their side, which leads to a grotesque mis­read­ing of the other side.

shelf.title: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Friedman’s short video ar­gu­ment that a min­i­mum wage doesn’t lift a low-productivity worker’s pay to the legal floor: it makes the job il­le­gal, so the wage drops to zero.

shelf.title: India Awakes
shelf.creator: Johan Norberg
shelf.why: Johan Norberg’s film tells Barun Mitra’s story of using satel­lite im­agery as court ev­i­dence to win land rights for trib­als, an in­spir­ing case of prop­erty rights chang­ing in­cen­tives on the ground.

shelf.title: The early Seen and the Unseen episode on demonetisation with Suyash Rai
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
shelf.why: An early episode with Suyash Rai, the source of his point that cost-benefit anal­y­sis hides an im­moral­ity when the costs fall on one group and the ben­e­fits on an­other.

laughs.text: When Amit men­tions a se­cret project, Ajay warns him: ‘the FSB, they scrape YouTube, they will hear the words. Secret project. And now they will start tap­ping your phone.’ Then he help­fully ex­plains that the FSB is the new name of the KGB.
Amit’s T-shirt line for the show’s merch: ‘Make trade not war.’ He fol­lows up by ask­ing whether Ajay prefers mak­ing trade or mak­ing love. The an­swer: ‘Unprintable.’

Amit says Ajay’s mentee is ‘turn­ing into an Ajay, which is rather alarming’, and asks how Ajay feels about young Ajays run­ning around the world. Ajay: they’ll soon get over the delu­sion that ‘there is any­thing here which is some­how spe­cial.’ Amit: ‘Oh my god, such mod­esty.’

Gunnar Myrdal, the Nobel-winning econ­o­mist who ar­gued that ma­chin­ery was good for the West but not for India be­cause de­mand for labour might fall. Amit’s ver­dict: ‘Dude wins the Nobel Prize for talk­ing this shit.’

Ajay re­calls the old line about bank rob­bers in the American West, ‘Why do you rob banks? Because that’s where the money is’, to ex­plain why gov­ern­ments ev­ery­where raid the fi­nan­cial sys­tem.
